top_level_objectives: Represent physical quantities with vectors that encode both magnitude and direction
Perform vector addition (tip-to-tail) and interpret the resultant’s magnitude and direction
Decompose a vector into perpendicular components and relate components to magnitude/direction using right-triangle trigonometry
Apply vector component ideas to projectile motion: identify constant horizontal velocity and changing vertical velocity under gravity
Predict and explain how launch angle and speed affect range and maximum height using 2D vector decomposition and kinematic reasoning

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce vectors as arrows carrying magnitude and direction and establish the idea of tip and tail as the “start” and “end” of a quantity.
key_visuals: A grid plane with an AR coordinate system (x horizontal, y vertical)
A movable “velocity vector” arrow with numeric readouts for magnitude and angle
Ghosted reference axes and a right-angle marker for later decomposition
A highlighted direction arc showing how angle defines the arrow orientation
student_actions: Select different magnitudes and directions for the displayed vector
Observe and record how changing direction (angle) rotates the arrow while changing magnitude stretches it
Estimate the vector’s component behavior by visually projecting the arrow toward the x and y axes (no formal decomposition yet)

scenes.brief_purpose: Build intuition for adding vectors geometrically and understanding the resultant as a single vector that combines effects.
key_visuals: Two draggable vectors displayed sequentially tip-to-tail
A resultant arrow from the start of the first vector to the end of the second vector
Angle/magnitude meters for each vector and the resultant
Optional dotted guide lines showing the parallelogram formed by two vectors
student_actions: Drag vector A then vector B so they connect tip-to-tail
Compare the resultant to the expected geometric sum by checking its measured magnitude and direction
Answer a quick prompt: which changes more strongly—resultant magnitude or direction—when you vary the direction of one addend

scenes.scene_name: Scene 3: Decomposing a Vector into Components
scenes.brief_purpose: Teach component decomposition along chosen axes and connect components to the original vector using right-triangle trigonometry.
key_visuals: A selected vector with perpendicular projections onto x and y axes
Right-triangle visualization with hypotenuse = vector magnitude and legs = |Vx| and |Vy|
Live component readouts Vx and Vy with sign (positive/negative) based on quadrant
Angle θ between the vector and the x-axis highlighted
student_actions: Choose axes (x and y) and decompose the displayed vector into components
Use the highlighted right triangle to relate Vx = V cosθ and Vy = V sinθ (conceptually, by verifying against readouts)
Change the vector angle while keeping magnitude fixed and predict how Vx and Vy respond

scenes.scene_name: Scene 4: From Components to 2D Projectile Motion
scenes.brief_purpose: Bridge vector decomposition to projectile motion by identifying initial velocity components and their distinct physical roles.
key_visuals: A projectile at launch with an initial velocity vector arrow at an arbitrary angle
Decomposition of that initial velocity into a horizontal component (constant) and vertical component (changing)
A side-view schematic showing gravity acting downward as a vector acceleration arrow
Two motion trackers: one for x-position vs time (uniform) and one for y-position vs time (accelerated)
student_actions: Set a launch angle and launch speed, then observe the decomposition into Vx and Vy
Trace the projectile path while watching the horizontal motion remain steady in speed/direction
Watch the vertical velocity change (sign and magnitude) during ascent vs descent and match it to the vertical component behavior

scenes.scene_name: Scene 5: Trajectory Emerges from Independent Motions
scenes.brief_purpose: Explain how the parabolic trajectory results from combining uniform horizontal motion with uniformly accelerated vertical motion.
key_visuals: Overlay of a “horizontal-only” ghost motion (straight line in x with constant speed) and a “vertical-only” ghost motion (free-fall style y change)
A combined trajectory curve (parabola) forming as the projectile advances
Coordinate markers showing x and y at selected time stamps
Optional animation of vector updates: horizontal displacement increments vs vertical displacement increments
student_actions: Step through time intervals and match the projectile’s (x,y) position to the two independent motions
Predict whether the projectile should be at the same x at equal time intervals (yes) and explain why y differs due to gravity
Complete a reasoning check: describe in words how the parabola’s shape follows from vertical acceleration

scenes.scene_name: Scene 6: Explore Angle and Speed Effects (Range & Maximum Height)
scenes.brief_purpose: Let students manipulate parameters and connect observed changes in range and maximum height to changes in Vx and Vy components.
key_visuals: Interactive controls for launch angle and launch speed
A trajectory display with labeled extrema: maximum height and landing point/range
Component bars for Vx and Vy updating instantly with angle/speed
Comparison mode to overlay multiple trajectories for different settings
student_actions: Run a set of trials changing angle at fixed speed; identify which component increases/decreases and relate it to maximum height and range
Run trials changing speed at fixed angle and explain which aspects scale more strongly (both components)
Select an angle that achieves a target range (or target max height) and justify the choice using component reasoning
